items.title: ​No, Neha didn’t use a guerrilla tactic, romanticising the term hurts dissent
items.summary: Did the All India Students’ Association (AISA) leader Neha Bora use a doppelganger to evade Delhi police during the October 11 protests? Neha clarified that she hadn’t set out to do that at all. “It was not a strategy but a simple coincidence," she said later the same day on Instagram. But social media and news platforms had already rushed to characterise a case of mistaken identities as a “strategy” or "battlefield tactic”. Neha was immediately showered in praise for cleverly “ outsmarting ” authorities. To call a coincidence a manoeuvre of war is a dangerous misrepresentation of facts. It leaves peaceful civilian protesters, most of them in their 20s and 30s, vulnerable to a narrative that frames nonviolent dissent as active combat. What happened? On October 11, the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) and various Left student bodies, including AISA, called for protests amid the demand for Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Neha asked protestors to gather at RK Ashram Marg in New Delhi at 2.30 pm. “See you there. Don’t be late,” she signed off. The number of protesters and journalists swelled at RK Ashram. As police tried to stop movement towards Jantar Mantar, chaos ensued. One protester, her face partially covered, was mistaken for Neha, chased down and detained. But Neha wasn’t at RK Ashram. Soon a second social media post from her announced that she and other AISA members had crossed the barricades into Connaught Place. She also shared dramatic visuals of her running alongside protesters to evade detention. While Neha was eventually detained and whisked away, the confusion about her location sparked social media posts and headlines congratulating her for "guerrilla warfare”. One report referred to the mixup as a "battlefield tactic” worthy of Neha’s upbringing by an army officer. The report claims she had intentionally “sent a doppelganger” so that police could chase a “deliberately planted look-alike”. Other reports talked of an ‘Asli (real) Neha” and “Nakli (fake) Neha”. Headlines screamed ‘How Neha Bora tricked Delhi Police with a Doppelganger’ and the ‘Tale of two Nehas’. These headlines took on a life of their own for hours before Neha could issue her clarification from a detention centre that it was all nothing more than a coincidence. The ‘look-alike’ had also been taken to the same detention centre from where the two women posted a photo together. Civil disobedience, not war Fluidity is in the nature of protest, particular
